newsitem.title: UK: Russia budget unlikely to pass - Nizhny governor.
newsitem.headline: Russia budget unlikely to pass - Nizhny governor.

text.p: The 1997 Russian budget draft is unlikely to get through the lower house this weekend, governor of Nizhny Novgorod Boris Nemtsov told reporters on Thursday.
The draft budget for next year is due to go through its first reading in the State Duma on Sunday.
"I'm not sure the budget will be adopted next week. Not because it's bad but because of political problems," said Nemtsov, who was on a brief official visit to Britain.
However, Nemtsov, who describes himself as a liberal, said it was hard to predict what might happen before the year ends.

The draft has to go through three readings in the Duma and be approved by the upper house before it can become law. If it fails to get approval, the government will be forced to use an interim budget or re-use the 1996 budget.
Analysts say passage of the budget could be crucial if the the International Monetary Fund is going to release more tranches of its $10 billion loan.
Nemtsov urged the government to deal with corruption, saying the country having chosen capitalism, had to decide whether it was to be democratic or corrupt.
Open tenders were one effective way of countering the problem.
But the authorities also need to deal with monopolies such as in transport and energy, make public policy more open and reform the military and legal structure.
Collection of taxes is also crucial if the government has any hope of reducing interest rates.
With local Treasury bills offering annual interest rates of close to 40 percent, it was invevitable that Russia's banks did not invest in industry, he added.
However, he ruled out any chance of the Russian federation breaking up.
Nemtsov pointed to the war in Chechnya and dependence on Moscow for commercial finance as factors which ensured the regions stuck together.
